title: The Senator Who Signed the Money: Mississippi, 1881 to Now | The Long View, Ep. 2
lede: Mississippi elected Scott Colom this week, its first Black U.S. senator since Blanche K. Bruce left the Senate in 1881. Bruce led the Senate's inquiry into the failed Freedman's Savings and Trust Company, then, as Register of the Treasury, signed the nation's paper money. This episode follows the question from 1870 to now: who gets a seat where the money is decided? Plus the week's African markets, October inflation, the Caribbean's citizenship deadline from Europe and the dates to watch.
keyPoints: AP called Mississippi's Senate race for Scott Colom on Nov 11; he led by 4,585 votes at the call, and Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded (AP, Democracy Docket).
U.S. consumer prices rose 0.4% in October; BLS published no 12-month rate because October 2025 prices were never collected during the shutdown (BLS, Nov 10).

Blanche K. Bruce chaired the Senate's 1879–80 inquiry into the Freedman's bank and served as Register of the Treasury from 1881 to 1885, with his signature on U.S. notes (U.S. House History, CoinWeek).
No African American served in the Senate for 86 years, from 1881 to 1967 (Congressional Research Service).
The EU wants five Caribbean citizenship-by-investment programmes ended by June 1, 2028; Antigua and Barbuda says it is prepared to end its own (Caribbean Today).
